questions.q: State the primary reason why ethanol (C₂H₅OH) has a higher boiling point than propane (C₃H₈) despite having nearly the same molecular mass (46 vs 44 g/mol).
questions.a: Ethanol has an –OH group enabling intermolecular hydrogen bonding, a strong dipole-dipole interaction, while propane is nonpolar and only experiences weak London dispersion forces. Hydrogen bonding requires significantly more energy to overcome, raising the boiling point. A wrong answer (e.g., "ethanol has higher molecular mass") reveals the student ignores intermolecular forces and focuses only on molar mass, a common Class 11 carryover error.

questions.q: Explain why the boiling point of butan-1-ol (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH) is higher than that of 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tert-butanol, (CH₃)₃COH), even though both have the same molecular formula C₄H₁₀O.
questions.a: Butan-1-ol is a straight-chain alcohol with larger surface area, leading to stronger van der Waals forces in addition to hydrogen bonding. Tert-butanol is highly branched (spherical), reducing surface area and weakening van der Waals forces. Both have similar H-bonding capacity (one –OH), so the difference arises from London forces. A wrong answer (e.g., "tert-butanol has more H-bonds") shows confusion about H-bonding sites — each molecule has only one –OH regardless of branching.

questions.q: Arrange the following in increasing order of boiling point: pentan-1-ol, n-butane, pentanal, ethoxyethane. Justify your ordering using intermolecular forces.
questions.a: n-Butane (only London forces) < ethoxyethane (dipole-dipole, no H-bond donor) < pentanal (dipole-dipole, no H-bond donor but larger dipole) < pentan-1-ol (intermolecular H-bonding). Pentan-1-ol has the highest bp due to H-bonding; ethoxyethane and pentanal have comparable masses but ethers have weaker polarity than aldehydes. A wrong ordering (e.g., placing pentanal above pentan-1-ol) indicates the student underestimates H-bonding strength relative to dipole-dipole interactions.

questions.q: Phenol (C₆H₅OH) has a boiling point of 455 K, while toluene (C₆H₅CH₃) boils at 384 K. Both have similar molecular masses (94 vs 92 g/mol). Analyze this difference in terms of molecular structure and intermolecular forces.
questions.a: Phenol has an –OH group directly attached to the sp² hybridised aromatic ring, allowing intermolecular hydrogen bonding and a net dipole moment. Toluene has a –CH₃ group, is nonpolar, and only experiences London forces. Despite similar mass, H-bonding in phenol dominates, giving a much higher boiling point. A wrong answer citing "phenyl group polarity" shows misunderstanding — the phenyl ring itself is nonpolar; the –OH group creates the polarity and H-bonding.

questions.q: A student claims: "All alcohols are miscible with water in all proportions because they have an –OH group." Evaluate this statement and correct it with a specific counterexample.
questions.a: The statement is false. Only lower molecular mass alcohols (methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol) are miscible in all proportions. As the alkyl chain lengthens (e.g., butan-1-ol, pentan-1-ol), the hydrophobic hydrocarbon portion dominates, reducing solubility. For example, butan-1-ol solubility is ~9 g/100 mL water, while hexan-1-ol is barely soluble (~0.6 g/100 mL). The student overlooks the increasing hydrophobic effect of the alkyl chain — a classic "functional group fixation" error.

questions.q: Design a simple laboratory experiment to demonstrate that branching in alcohols lowers boiling point, using only common lab chemicals (butan-1-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol, thermometer, heat source). Outline the procedure, expected observations, and the conclusion linking structure to property.
questions.a: Procedure: Place 5 mL of butan-1-ol in a test tube with a thermometer, heat gently in a water bath, record boiling point. Repeat with 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Observation: Butan-1-ol boils at ~390 K, tert-butanol at ~356 K. Conclusion: Both have same formula (C₄H₁₀O) and one –OH group, so H-bonding is similar. The lower bp of tert-butanol is due to its compact, branched structure reducing surface area and weakening London dispersion forces. A poor design (e.g., open flame heating) reveals safety ignorance; a vague conclusion ("branching changes bp") shows lack of mechanistic reasoning.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Physical properties of alcohols and phenols refer to their observable ______ such as boiling points, solubility, and molecular geometry that arise from the presence of the hydroxyl (–OH) group attached to an aliphatic (alcohols) or aromatic (phenols) carbon chain.
Fill in the blank: Observe how ethanol (in hand sanitizer) evaporates quickly but leaves a cooling sensation, while water evaporates slower — both have –OH groups but different ______ masses.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to: (1) Predict and explain trends in boiling points of alcohols/phenols based on molecular mass, branching, and hydrogen bonding; (2) Predict and explain solubility trends in water based on the size of the alkyl/aryl group; (3) Compare physical properties of alcohols, phenols, ethers, and hydrocarbons of.
